darshana: In Indian philosophy, a darshana is a systematic school of thought, a comprehensive 'view' of reality that combines doctrine with a path of practice aimed at liberation. Classical usage counts six orthodox darshanas — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta — which accept the authority of the Vedas, while Buddhist, Jain, and materialist Carvaka schools stand outside that group as rival views. The Sanskrit word derives from a root meaning 'to see,' so each darshana is in effect a distinct way of seeing and organizing experience.
vedic-sacrifice: Yajna, the ritual sacrifice, was the central religious act of Vedic India (roughly 1500-500 BCE): offerings of ghee, grain, and the pressed soma juice poured into the sacred fire by specially trained Brahmin priests. The rite was believed to sustain the gods and thereby uphold cosmic and social order, and elaborate manuals prescribed its correct performance down to each gesture and utterance. Later philosophical reflection transformed it: the Upanishads reinterpreted sacrifice inwardly, while the Mimamsa school made Vedic ritual the very foundation of dharma and held its efficacy to be eternal and self-sufficient.
dependent-origination: Pratityasamutpada, the principle of dependent origination, is the Buddha's central causal teaching: every phenomenon arises only in dependence on other conditions and ceases when those conditions cease, so nothing exists as an independent, self-standing thing. The classic formulation traces twelve links (nidanas), beginning with ignorance, that explain how craving, clinging, and rebirth produce suffering. Because all things are conditioned in this way, the principle grounds the Buddhist doctrines of no-self and, in later Madhyamaka thought, emptiness.
abhidharma: The Abhidharma is the scholastic literature, developing from about the third century BCE, in which Buddhist thinkers analyzed the Buddha's discourses into their ultimate constituents: impermanent, momentary events called dharmas, such as particular instances of color, feeling, or consciousness. On this analysis a person is not a substantial self but a causally connected stream of such dharmas, which explains continuity without positing a soul. Schools such as the Sarvastivada and the Theravadins built rival taxonomies of dharmas, producing the systematic metaphysics that later Buddhist philosophy, including Yogacara, both developed and contested.
yogacara-mind-only: Yogacara, the Buddhist school that flourished from about the fourth century CE and is associated with the half-brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu, is known for its doctrine of 'mind-only' (cittamatra) or 'representation-only.' It holds that the objects we experience are constructions of consciousness: we never encounter a world outside our mental representations, which arise from seeds stored in a subconscious 'storehouse consciousness' (alaya-vijnana). The doctrine was meant less as a denial that experience occurs than as an account of how the mistaken belief in an independent external world sustains suffering.
classical-yoga: Classical Yoga is the system codified in the Yoga Sutras, traditionally attributed to the compiler Patanjali and dated somewhere between the second century BCE and the fourth century CE. It prescribes an eight-limbed path (ashtanga) running from ethical restraints and observances through posture, breath control, and sensory withdrawal to progressively deeper states of concentration, meditation, and absorption (samadhi). Sharing the dualist metaphysics of Samkhya, it holds that suffering comes from misidentifying conscious spirit with nature, and that disciplined practice leads to kaivalya, the liberation of the seer from the seen.
samkhya-dualism: Samkhya, often regarded as the oldest of the classical Indian schools and traditionally ascribed to the sage Kapila, is a dualism of purusha and prakriti. Purusha designates the plurality of conscious selves, pure witnesses that are never agents, while prakriti is primordial material nature, composed of three strands (sattva, rajas, and tamas) and capable of evolving into mind, senses, and the physical world. Suffering arises because the self mistakenly identifies with nature's products; liberation comes through discriminating knowledge that separates the witness from what is witnessed, a position classically stated in Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika.
vaisheshika-categories: The Vaisheshika school, traditionally founded by the sage Kanada, developed an atomistic realism organized around an enumeration of the padarthas, the categories into which everything that can be named falls. The classic list has seven members: substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and, added in later systematization, non-existence or absence. Particularity (vishesha) is the category that individuates ultimate atoms, which the school held to be eternal, indivisible particles of earth, water, fire, and air, making Vaisheshika one of the earliest sustained atomic theories.
nyaya-five-limb-inference: The Nyaya school, whose foundational sutras are attributed to Aksapada Gautama, analyzed inference (anumana) into five members, a schema that functions both as a proof and as a fully explicit argument. A standard example: the mountain has fire (thesis); because it has smoke (reason); whatever has smoke has fire, like a kitchen and unlike a lake (example stating the universal concomitance); this mountain has smoke (application); therefore it has fire (conclusion). The five-membered form remained central to Indian logic and formal debate and was later adapted by Buddhist logicians such as Dignaga and Dharmakirti.
mimamsa: Mimamsa, or Purva Mimamsa, is the Indian school devoted to interpreting the ritual portions of the Vedas, founded on Jaimini's sutras in roughly the last centuries BCE. It defines dharma as what the Vedic injunctions prescribe and defends the Vedas as eternal and unauthored, hence an infallible source of knowledge. In developing its hermeneutics the school produced sophisticated work on language, meaning, and sentence interpretation, and its later masters Kumarila and Prabhakara became major philosophers in their own right, with an epistemology that strongly influenced Vedanta.
semiotics-signifier-signified: Semiotics is the general theory of signs and of how they convey meaning, developed along two main lines: Ferdinand de Saussure's linguistics and Charles Sanders Peirce's logic of signs. Saussure modeled the sign as a union of signifier (the sound-pattern or written mark) and signified (the concept it expresses), insisting that the link between them is arbitrary and that signs mean what they do only through their differences from other signs within a system. That framework underlay structuralist and post-structuralist analyses of culture, in which everything from myth to fashion could be read as a system of signs.
anti-psychologism: Anti-psychologism is the thesis, argued most influentially by Gottlob Frege, that the laws of logic and mathematics are objective truths about concepts, numbers, and validity, not generalizations about how human minds happen to think. The opposing psychologism, prominent in nineteenth-century empiricism, treated logical laws as empirical laws of thought, a view Frege attacked for confusing the grounds of a truth with the psychological causes of holding it. Edmund Husserl delivered a parallel critique in his Logical Investigations, and the resulting separation of logic from psychology became a cornerstone of both analytic philosophy and phenomenology.
intrinsic-vs-instrumental-value: Value theorists distinguish things that are good for their own sake from things that are good as means to something else: pleasure or happiness is often held to be intrinsically valuable, while money or medicine is instrumentally valuable, worth having only because of what it leads to. The distinction, sharpened in the early twentieth century by G. E. Moore's 'isolation test' for intrinsic value, structures debates in ethics about what makes a life or an action ultimately worthwhile. Borderline cases, such as knowledge, achievement, and the value of persons, have kept the analysis of the distinction a live topic.
sorites-paradox: The sorites paradox — from the Greek soros, 'heap' — was posed by the ancient philosopher Eubulides of Miletus: one grain of sand is not a heap, and adding a single grain to what is not a heap cannot make a heap; iterating the reasoning yields that a million grains do not make a heap, which is plainly absurd. The puzzle exposes the problem of vague predicates like 'heap,' 'bald,' and 'tall,' which admit borderline cases and appear to lack sharp boundaries. Contemporary responses include epistemicism, which holds that there are hidden sharp boundaries, and supervaluationism, which preserves ordinary speech while denying that 'heap' has a precise extension.
maternal-thinking: Maternal thinking is the account developed by the American philosopher Sara Ruddick in her 1989 book Maternal Thinking, which presents mothering not merely as labor or feeling but as an intellectual practice that generates its own characteristic ways of thought. The demands of keeping children safe and fostering their growth cultivate attention, humility, and concrete judgment, together with an ethics of preservation, growth, and training that can conflict with abstract principle. Ruddick stressed that 'maternal' names a social practice rather than a biological role, so men can mother, and she argued that the practice carries implications for peace politics as well.
original-sin: Original sin is the Christian doctrine that the transgression of the first human beings, classically Adam's disobedience, wounded human nature itself, so that all descendants are born with an inherited condition inclining them to sin and death. Augustine of Hippo gave the Western church its definitive account, arguing that Adam's guilt and corruption are transmitted to every person and can be remedied only by grace; Pelagius, who denied that Adam's sin damaged his descendants in this way, was condemned as a heretic. Eastern Orthodox theology, by contrast, has generally understood the inheritance as mortality and corruption rather than shared guilt.
parasocial-relationship: The term parasocial relationship was introduced by the media researchers Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl in 1956 to describe the one-sided intimacy television viewers developed with performers, who felt like familiar friends although the relationship ran entirely in one direction. The concept has since been extended to celebrities, influencers, live streamers, and fictional characters, covering the sense of knowing someone who cannot know you in return. Philosophically, such attachments raise questions about authenticity, the ethics of commercially manufactured intimacy, and whether parasocial bonds are a diminished substitute for, or a genuine form of, friendship.
reputation: In social epistemology, reputation refers to the circulating beliefs and evaluations a community holds about a person, which function as testimony: others rely on a reputation to decide whom to trust, hire, or believe before any direct evidence is available. Because reputations can be inaccurate, slow to correct, and shaped by prejudice, they raise questions of fairness — a person can be treated on the strength of false information — and of epistemic justice, since whose word counts often depends on whose reputation stands. Philosophers study how reputational systems, from honor cultures to online ratings, distribute credibility and how they might be reformed.
repetition-and-difference: In Difference and Repetition (1968), Gilles Deleuze argues that repetition is never the mere return of the same: every genuine repetition produces a difference, because it always occurs under conditions of displacement and disguise. Against the philosophical tradition that treats identity as primary and difference as merely derivative, Deleuze reverses the order, making difference-in-itself the fundamental character of reality and of thought. The book is widely read as a rejection of representation — of thinking modeled on the recognition of the same — in favor of thought that registers the new.
archive-fever: Archive fever (mal d'archive) is the title concept of a 1995 lecture by Jacques Derrida, drawing on Freud, which names the double compulsion at the heart of collecting and preserving: the drive to secure the past in a place of custody, and the destructive 'fever' of forgetting that is inseparable from it. Derrida ties the archive to a founding violence — the authority of those who decide what counts as archivable — and argues that the archive's technology (he wrote amid the rise of email) conditions what future memory and future scholarship can be. The piece became a touchstone for theories of memory, history, and documentation.
philosophy-of-grief: The philosophy of grief examines the nature, rationality, and value of mourning: whether grief involves irrational beliefs, as Freud suggested in the survivor's refusal to accept the death; whether painful emotions over losses can be fitting rather than mere pathology; and what grief reveals about our attachments and identity. Contemporary analytic work often treats grief as a form of love that persists beyond death and reshapes the griever's commitments, asking how one can live well while honoring the dead. The topic draws on the Stoics, Augustine, and Spinoza as much as on current philosophy of emotion.
affective-injustice: Affective injustice names wrongs done to people in their emotional lives — for example, when an emotional culture privileges the feelings of some groups while shaming or silencing the emotions of others, or when emotions apt to one's situation, such as anger at oppression, are dismissed as irrational or unprofessional. The idea builds on feminist work such as Alison Jaggar's account of 'outlaw emotions,' feelings that detect injustice the dominant view misses, and on recent analyses of whose affect is permitted public expression. Philosophers use the concept to argue that justice concerns not only material goods and rights but the fair standing of people's emotional capacities.
philosophy-of-anger: The philosophy of anger asks what anger is, when it is justified, and whether it does moral good or harm. The Stoics, especially Seneca, condemned it as a temporary madness and a desire for revenge; Aristotle, by contrast, counted a fitting anger at real slights as part of virtuous character. The contemporary debate renews both positions: some philosophers defend anger at injustice as apt, communicative, and motivating, while others argue, with Martha Nussbaum, that its retributive element makes a forward-looking 'transitional' anger the better moral instrument.
standpoint-epistemology: Feminist standpoint epistemology holds that knowledge is socially situated: what one can perceive and know depends on one's position in relations of labor and power. Drawing on Marx's account of the proletarian standpoint, theorists such as Nancy Hartsock and Sandra Harding argued that the perspectives of marginalized groups, achieved through collective political struggle, can be epistemically advantaged, because the view from below exposes social relations that the dominant standpoint renders invisible. Harding's slogan of 'strong objectivity' claims that starting inquiry from marginalized lives produces more, not less, rigorous knowledge.
beauty-myth: The beauty myth is the thesis advanced by Naomi Wolf in her 1990 book of that name: that as women won legal and economic equality, a rising ideology of female beauty — thinner, younger, ever more unattainable images — was deployed to keep women anxious, competitive, and preoccupied, functioning as a political and economic constraint where older barriers had fallen. Wolf argued that the ideal is not about beauty itself but about control, operating across work, religion, sex, and violence alike. The book was criticized on points of evidence but became a touchstone of feminist analysis of body norms and the beauty industries.
reproductive-justice: Reproductive justice is a framework formulated in 1994 by a coalition of Black women activists, notably Loretta Ross and the group SisterSong, as an alternative to a politics focused solely on abortion rights. It asserts three human rights: the right to have children, the right not to have children, and the right to parent children in safe and sustainable communities, with access to the conditions — economic security, health care, freedom from violence — that make those choices real. The framework insists that legal access without the social means to act is incomplete, and it centers the experience of women of color and poor women.
race-as-social-construct: The claim that race is a social construct holds that races are not natural divisions of humankind marked by biological essence, but kinds constituted by historical, legal, and political practices — slavery, classification, segregation — that nonetheless make race real in its effects. The position traces to W. E. B. Du Bois and has been elaborated by philosophers such as Kwame Anthony Appiah and Sally Haslanger, who debate whether racial categories are illusions to be eliminated or social identities worth retaining for the sake of justice. The constructivist view explains both why biology finds no racial genes dividing humanity and why racism produces measurable social and bodily harms.
wrongful-discrimination: In philosophy, wrongful discrimination is a term of art for differential treatment on grounds such as race, sex, or religion that is wrong — since not all discrimination is: selecting the more qualified candidate is discrimination of an innocent kind. The central question is what makes the wrongful kind wrong. Deborah Hellman has argued that discrimination wrongs people when it demeans them by denying equal social standing, while Benjamin Eidelson locates the wrong in treating people as inferior in worth; the debate extends to indirect discrimination and statistical profiling.
speech-acts: Speech act theory, founded in J. L. Austin's 1962 lectures How to Do Things with Words, studies utterances that perform actions rather than merely describe the world: saying 'I promise,' 'I apologize,' or 'I now pronounce you married' is doing something, and it succeeds only under felicity conditions such as the right authority and circumstances. Austin distinguished the act of saying something (locutionary), the act performed in saying it (illocutionary), and its effects on hearers (perlocutionary), and John Searle systematized the taxonomy of illocutionary acts. Feminist philosophers such as Rae Langton later used the theory to analyze how pornography can silence women's speech.
mimetic-desire: Mimetic desire is the central idea of the French-American thinker René Girard: human beings do not desire objects spontaneously but imitate the desires of others, learning what to want from models or mediators. Because the model becomes a rival for the same object, imitative desire breeds conflict — mimetic rivalry — so desire is triangular, running from subject through model to object. Girard developed the theory through readings of Cervantes, Stendhal, Proust, and Dostoevsky in Deceit, Desire, and the Novel (1961), and extended it into a general theory of social conflict.
scapegoat-mechanism: The scapegoat mechanism is René Girard's account of how human communities escape the self-destructive spiral of imitative rivalry: when mimetic violence threatens a society with all-against-all conflict, it is resolved by the collective killing or expulsion of a single victim, whose death restores peace. The victim, once the source of disorder, becomes the source of order and hence sacred, generating myth, ritual, and religious sacrifice — a thesis argued in Violence and the Sacred (1972). Girard held that the Hebrew scriptures and the Gospels uniquely expose the mechanism by telling these stories from the point of view of the innocent victim.
becoming-other: Becoming is a central notion in the philosophy of Gilles Deleuze, developed with Félix Guattari in A Thousand Plateaus: processes of transformation in which a being passes into what it is not — becoming-woman, becoming-animal, becoming-molecular — without imitating or resembling its target. A becoming occurs in a 'zone of indiscernibility' where two terms exchange elements and both are changed, producing new possibilities rather than preserving fixed identities. The concept underwrites Deleuze's broader attack on identity as the foundation of thought and politics, and his preference for lines of flight over stable structures.
open-interpretation: Open interpretation is the view, prominent in hermeneutics and literary theory, that a text legitimately admits more than one defensible reading rather than a single correct meaning fixed by its author. Umberto Eco's idea of the 'open work' and Roland Barthes's proclamation of the 'death of the author' gave the view its classic formulations, with Barthes locating meaning in language and the reader rather than authorial intention. The debate then turned on limits: Eco himself later argued against unlimited semiosis, insisting that while texts are plural, interpretations can still be shown to be wrong.
popular-parody: Popular parody is the branch of parody that takes popular culture as its object and addresses a mass audience, as distinct from the 'art parody' of elite tradition. Parody theory, notably Linda Hutcheon's account of parody as 'repetition with critical distance' and Margaret Rose's work on the form, emphasizes that parody ranges from ridicule to reverent homage: a popular parody typically reproduces the conventions of a genre or text with a difference that both honors and comments on the original. The form raises questions about the boundary between critique and mere copying, and about what changes when the source is itself already commercial.
phil:panini: Panini was a Sanskrit grammarian of northern India, conventionally dated to the fourth century BCE, whose Astadhyayi (Eight Chapters) is one of the most remarkable intellectual achievements of the ancient world. The work compresses the grammar of the Sanskrit language into roughly four thousand terse rules (sutras), organized with meta-rules and ordering conventions so that, given a stem and an ending, the correct form can be derived mechanically. Scholars regard it as a generative system comparable in power to modern formal grammars, and it remained the authoritative description of Sanskrit for all later Indian linguistic and philosophical work.
phil:ramanuja: Ramanuja (1017-1137) was a South Indian theologian-philosopher, the greatest exponent of Vishishtadvaita, the 'qualified non-dualism' school of Vedanta. Against Shankara's doctrine that the world of souls and matter is ultimately illusory, Ramanuja held that individual selves and the material world are real, forming the body of a personal God, Vishnu, who is the sole independent reality. He wrote the Sribhashya, an influential commentary on the Brahma Sutras, and made loving devotion (bhakti) to God the path to liberation, shaping the devotional Srivaishnava tradition of South India.
phil:arthur-danto: Arthur Danto (1924-2013) was an American philosopher and art critic who taught for decades at Columbia University. His 1964 essay 'The Artworld,' prompted by Warhol's Brillo Box, argued that what makes an object art is not how it looks but its relation to the artworld's theories and history: two visually indistinguishable objects can differ in that one is art and the other is not. Danto went on to define artworks as embodied meanings — artifacts that are about something and express that meaning in their form — and to argue, after Hegel, that art had entered a post-historical condition of pluralism in which its narrative of progressive development had ended.
phil:linda-zagzebski: Linda Zagzebski is a contemporary American philosopher, long at the University of Oklahoma, best known for developing virtue epistemology, which models intellectual evaluation on virtue ethics: knowledge is understood as arising from acts of intellectual virtue such as conscientiousness and open-mindedness (Virtues of the Mind, 1996). In later work she advanced exemplarism, the theory that moral and epistemic concepts are anchored in our direct admiration of exemplary persons, presented in Exemplarist Moral Theory (2017). She has also written extensively on divine foreknowledge, fatalism, and the nature of epistemic authority.
phil:heather-widdows: Heather Widdows is a British philosopher at the University of Birmingham known for work in global ethics, bioethics, and the philosophy of beauty. In Perfect Me! Beauty as an Ethical Ideal (2018) she argues that the contemporary beauty ideal — thinness, youth, smooth skin — has become a dominant moral ideal demanding work and discipline like other moral projects, so that beauty practices require ethical evaluation rather than dismissal as trivial. She has also written on the ethics of infectious disease, global health, and the methodology of ethics across borders.
phil:paul-ricoeur: Paul Ricoeur (1913-2005) was a French philosopher who worked at the crossing point of phenomenology and hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation. His wide-ranging work included studies of the will and evil, a landmark interpretation of Freud, the philosophy of metaphor in The Rule of Metaphor, and the three-volume Time and Narrative, which examined how humans configure time through stories and developed the notion of narrative identity — the self as told rather than merely found. He placed Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud at the origin of a 'hermeneutics of suspicion,' and also wrote on justice, translation, and personal identity in Oneself as Another.
phil:michael-cholbi: Michael Cholbi is a contemporary American philosopher known as one of the leading philosophers of grief and of suicide. His book Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) argues that grief is a form of love for the departed that reorients the griever's own commitments, and that the pain of grief is rational rather than a malfunction to be cured. He has also written on the ethics of suicide, Kantian ethics, punishment, and bioethics, and has helped establish the philosophy of death and dying as a recognized research field.
phil:edith-stein: Edith Stein (1891-1942) was a German philosopher, a student and later assistant of Edmund Husserl whose dissertation On the Problem of Empathy (1917) remains a classic phenomenological study of how we apprehend the experiences of other subjects. After converting from Judaism to Catholicism in 1922, she sought to integrate phenomenology with Thomist metaphysics in Finite and Eternal Being, while also writing on women's education and social philosophy. She entered a Carmelite convent as Sister Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, was arrested during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, and died at Auschwitz in 1942; she was canonized in 1998.
phil:w-d-ross: W. D. Ross (1877-1971) was a Scottish philosopher at Oxford, an eminent Aristotle scholar whose translation of the Nicomachean Ethics remains widely used. In The Right and the Good (1930) he proposed that morality is a plurality of 'prima facie duties' — fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence, and self-improvement — genuine duties that can conflict, with no single master principle to settle the conflicts; judgment must weigh them case by case. This pluralist deontology was a major alternative to utilitarianism and to Kantian monism and remains central to normative ethics.
phil:peter-geach: Peter Geach (1916-2013) was a British analytic philosopher who studied under Wittgenstein at Cambridge and taught at Birmingham and Leeds. He worked on logic, reference, and predication — his Reference and Generality (1962) is a classic study of quantification — and advanced the 'relative identity' thesis that identity statements are always relative to a sortal term. A devout Catholic and Thomist, he and his wife, the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe, wrote Three Philosophers together on Aristotle, Aquinas, and Frege, helping bring scholastic ideas into dialogue with analytic philosophy.
phil:helene-cixous: Hélène Cixous, born in 1937 in Oran, French Algeria, is a French writer and theorist associated with the feminist theory of écriture féminine, or feminine writing. In her 1975 essay 'The Laugh of the Medusa' she called on women to write their bodies and their desire, against a phallocentric literary tradition that had defined them as lacking, and she linked writing, sexuality, and subversion. A prolific novelist and critic, she was among the founders of the experimental University of Paris VIII at Vincennes, and her work spans deconstruction, psychoanalysis, and readings of writers from Clarice Lispector to James Joyce.
phil:ibram-x-kendi: Ibram X. Kendi, born in 1982, is an American historian and public scholar of racism and antiracism, author of Stamped from the Beginning (2016), which won the National Book Award, and How to Be an Antiracist (2019). He defines racism strictly at the level of ideas and policies: a racist idea is any that asserts one racial group is superior or inferior, and a racist policy is one that produces racial inequity, so the relevant divide is between racist and antiracist rather than between racist and 'not racist.' He founded the Center for Antiracist Research at Boston University, and his work has shaped both scholarship and public debate.
phil:reinhold-niebuhr: Reinhold Niebuhr (1892-1971) was an American Protestant theologian and social ethicist, the leading figure of Christian realism. In Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) he argued that individuals may be capable of selflessness but social groups almost always act from self-interest and power, so moral idealism is a poor guide to politics and justice must be pursued through balances of power rather than pure love. Works such as The Nature and Destiny of Man and his influence on postwar American liberalism made him one of the most consequential religious thinkers of the twentieth century; the Serenity Prayer is attributed to him.
phil:axel-honneth: Axel Honneth, born in 1949, is a German philosopher and a third-generation representative of the Frankfurt School of critical theory, directing its Institute for Social Research from 2001 to 2018. His central work, The Struggle for Recognition (1992), grounds social critique in three spheres of recognition — love in intimate relations, rights as a legal person, and solidarity or esteem for one's contributions — arguing that social conflicts and movements are best understood as struggles against recognition withheld in one of these forms. He has since developed a normative reconstruction of freedom in Freedom's Right and written on reification, capitalism, and democracy.
phil:thomas-paine: Thomas Paine (1737-1809) was an English-born pamphleteer and radical political thinker who became one of the intellectual voices of both the American and French revolutions. His pamphlet Common Sense (1776) did much to turn colonial opinion toward independence, while Rights of Man (1791-92), his reply to Edmund Burke's attack on the French Revolution, defended natural rights and popular sovereignty and proposed social measures such as old-age pensions. In The Age of Reason he set out a deist critique of organized and revealed religion, and in Agrarian Justice he sketched an early argument for universal payments funded by landowners, anticipating the welfare state.
phil:ruth-benedict: Ruth Benedict (1887-1948) was an American cultural anthropologist, a student and close colleague of Franz Boas at Columbia, whose Patterns of Culture (1934) became one of the most influential works of the discipline. Arguing that cultures are integrated wholes — she contrasted the 'Apollonian' Zuni with the 'Dionysian' Dobu — she held that traits and values make sense only within their configuration, and drew from this a case for cultural relativism in ethics: what counts as normal and good is defined differently in different cultures. Her The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946), a study of Japanese culture written during the war without fieldwork, shaped both anthropology and American understanding of Japan.
phil:malinowski: Bronislaw Malinowski (1884-1942) was a Polish-born anthropologist working in Britain who is regarded as the founder of modern ethnographic fieldwork. Through extended immersive residence among the Trobriand Islanders, described in Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), he established the method of participant observation: learning the local language, living among the people, and grasping the 'native's point of view' rather than collecting artifacts and reports at a distance. His functionalism explained institutions by the needs — biological, social, and symbolic — they satisfy, and his fieldwork model became the defining method of social anthropology.
phil:graham-greene: Graham Greene (1904-1991) was an English novelist whose fiction, though not academic philosophy, stands among the most serious literary explorations of faith, sin, and moral ambiguity of the twentieth century. In novels such as Brighton Rock, The Power and the Glory, The Heart of the Matter, and The End of the Affair he dramatized flawed and even wicked characters caught between belief and doubt, asking whether pity, love, and conscience can corrupt as well as save. He also wrote fast-paced 'entertainments' such as The Third Man and political novels set in Vietnam, Haiti, and Latin America, and his recurring theme — the shabbiness of devoted belief — made him a lasting reference in discussions of moral psychology.
phil:linda-hutcheon: Linda Hutcheon is a Canadian literary theorist at the University of Toronto whose work has defined the study of parody, postmodernism, and adaptation. In A Theory of Parody (1985) she characterized parody as 'repetition with critical distance,' a form ranging from reverent homage to ridicule that marks difference at the heart of similarity; in A Poetics of Postmodernism (1988) she coined the term 'historiographic metafiction' for fiction that self-consciously rewrites history; and in A Theory of Adaptation (2006) she analyzed adaptation as 'repetition without replication' across media.
